anxiety-signs-and-treatment.name: Anxiety: signs, treatment and getting help
anxiety-signs-and-treatment.summary: Anxiety becomes a health problem when worry is hard to control and affects daily life. Talking therapy comes first, medicine is next, and help is available without a GP referral.
keyPoints: Some anxiety is a normal part of life; it becomes a concern when worry is hard to control and gets in the way of daily life.
Adults are usually advised to try psychological treatment, such as cognitive behavioural therapy, before medicine.
People in England can refer themselves to an NHS talking therapies service without seeing a GP first.
If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 offer urgent support.

body.heading: What is anxiety, and when does it become a problem?
body.body: Feeling anxious now and then is part of life, and the NHS says some anxiety is normal. Generalised anxiety disorder, or GAD, is a long-term condition in which a person feels worried or stressed much of the time, about many things, in a way that is hard to control. That worry gets in the way of daily life.

body.heading: What are the signs?
body.body: Alongside worry, the NHS lists sleep difficulties, restlessness or irritability, tiredness, muscle tension, stomach problems, palpitations (a pounding or fluttering heartbeat), dizziness and low mood. Because many of these also occur in other conditions, a GP can help work out what is going on.

body.heading: What causes it?
body.body: The exact cause of GAD is not fully understood, and several factors probably combine. Factors named in the sources include inherited genes, past stressful or traumatic experiences, a long-term painful health condition, and past drug or alcohol misuse.

body.heading: What happens at the GP appointment?
body.body: NICE advises a full assessment that looks at how many symptoms there are, how severe they are, how long the current episode has lasted and how the condition has developed over time. The GP also asks about distress, the effect on daily functioning, and any past history of anxiety and mood disorders. Where another condition such as depression is also present, NICE says the more severe disorder is generally treated first. A short two-question screen about feelings of anxiety and the ability to control worry may be used.

body.heading: What does treatment involve?
body.body: Adults are usually advised to try psychological treatment before medication. Cognitive behavioural therapy, or CBT, is a talking therapy that looks at how thoughts, feelings and actions affect one another. The NHS describes CBT as one of the most effective treatments for GAD, and CBT and applied relaxation are both available on the NHS. NICE describes CBT-based self-help as a first, low-intensity step, with the materials worked through step by step over several weeks. If talking therapy is not enough, medicine is the next option, and the usual first choice is an SSRI, a type of antidepressant. NICE sets out treatment in steps, starting with identification, assessment, education about the condition and treatment options, and active monitoring. Step 4 is for complex, treatment-resistant anxiety with marked impairment or a high risk of self-harm, and involves specialist care.

body.heading: What can people do themselves?
body.body: NHS self-help ideas include regular exercise, relaxation or breathing practice, cutting back on caffeine, which can disrupt sleep, and eating well. The NHS advises against turning to alcohol, cigarettes, gambling or drugs to relieve anxiety. Many books and courses can teach ways of coping with anxiety.

body.heading: When should someone see a GP?
body.body: The NHS says to see a GP if anxiety is affecting daily life or causing distress. A GP can talk through treatment and refer on, and people can also refer themselves directly to an NHS talking therapies service. Charities such as Mind, Rethink Mental Illness and Anxiety UK also offer support.

body.heading: Where can someone get urgent help?
body.body: Anxiety is common and treatable, and most people will not need emergency help. If things feel unmanageable, these routes are open. If you or someone else is in immediate danger, or has been physically harmed, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), which trusts describe as available at any time, for yourself or on someone else's behalf. Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.

depression-signs-and-getting-help.name: Depression: signs and getting help
depression-signs-and-getting-help.summary: Depression is more than feeling unhappy for a few days. The NHS describes lasting low mood and loss of interest, and treatment can include self-help, talking therapy and medicine.
keyPoints: Depression is more than feeling unhappy or fed up for a few days, and it can come with physical symptoms.
Treatment depends on severity and usually combines self-help, talking therapies and sometimes medicine.
People can refer themselves to an NHS talking therapies service, or a GP can refer them.
If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 offer urgent support.

body.heading: What is depression?
body.body: The NHS describes depression as more than simply feeling unhappy or fed up for a few days. It can involve lasting feelings of unhappiness and hopelessness, and losing interest in things that used to be enjoyed.

body.heading: What are the signs?
body.body: Some people also notice physical symptoms, such as feeling constantly tired, sleeping badly, or having no appetite or sex drive. Because depression affects people differently, the NHS suggests a GP appointment for anyone who is concerned about how long these feelings have lasted. The NHS says a low mood that lasts for two weeks or more could be a sign of depression. Other symptoms it lists include getting no enjoyment out of life, feeling hopeless, being unable to concentrate on everyday things, and having thoughts about harming yourself or suicidal thoughts. Aches and pains can also be part of the picture. Depression can be mild or severe, and severe depression can bring a feeling that life is no longer worth living.

body.heading: What causes it?
body.body: Life-changing events such as bereavement, losing a job or giving birth can bring depression on. People with a family history of depression are more likely to experience it, and depression can also arise for no obvious reason.

body.heading: How is it treated?
body.body: Treatment usually depends on how severe the depression is. It usually involves a combination of self-help, talking therapies and medicine. For mild depression, a GP can refer someone for talking therapies, or the person can refer themselves directly to an NHS talking therapies service. For moderate to severe depression, a combination of talking therapy and antidepressants is often recommended. People with severe depression may be referred to a mental health team of psychologists, psychiatrists, specialist nurses and occupational therapists. For mild depression, a doctor may suggest watchful waiting, which means monitoring progress to see whether it improves, alongside lifestyle measures and guided self-help. The NHS says even moderate exercise releases chemicals in the brain that lift mood, and that working through a CBT-based self-help guide is an option. A NICE-based summary says antidepressants should not be offered as the main treatment for less severe depression unless that is the person's preference.

body.heading: How do antidepressants fit in?
body.body: Antidepressants are one option within that package, usually prescribed after a conversation with a GP. The NHS says symptoms start to improve some weeks after starting an antidepressant, so effects are not immediate. The NHS advises that antidepressants are reduced gradually when they are stopped, to help avoid withdrawal symptoms, and that this should be done with the GP. The NHS says to contact a GP straight away if feelings of hopelessness or suicidal thoughts start, or get worse, after starting an antidepressant.

body.heading: When should someone get help?
body.body: A GP appointment is the usual first step for someone who thinks they may have depression. NHS talking therapies accept self-referral, so a GP is not the only way in.

body.heading: Where can someone get urgent help?
body.body: Many people recover with the right support. If thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life are present, help is available immediately. If you or someone else is in immediate danger, or has been physically harmed, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), which trusts describe as available at any time, for yourself or on someone else's behalf. Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.

panic-attacks-what-they-are.name: Panic attacks: what they are and what helps
panic-attacks-what-they-are.summary: A panic attack is a rush of intense fear with physical symptoms such as a racing heartbeat. The NHS describes how attacks pass and how talking therapy and medicine can treat repeated attacks.
keyPoints: A panic attack causes physical symptoms such as a racing heartbeat, dizziness, sweating, trembling and shortness of breath, along with a sense of dread.
The NHS says a panic attack usually passes within minutes, and that fighting it often makes it worse.
Cognitive behavioural therapy is the main talking therapy for repeated panic attacks, and NHS talking therapies accept self-referral.
If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 offer urgent support.

body.heading: What is a panic attack?
body.body: A panic attack is a sudden rush of intense fear or anxiety. A single panic attack does not necessarily mean someone has panic disorder, which is when attacks keep coming back.

body.heading: What does it feel like?
body.body: Common physical signs are a racing heartbeat, dizziness, sweating, trembling, shortness of breath and nausea, along with a sense of dread. The NHS says a panic attack usually lasts between 5 and 20 minutes. Other symptoms the NHS lists include feeling faint, chest pain, hot flushes, chills, numbness or pins and needles, and a dry mouth. Many of these symptoms overlap with those of other conditions, so a GP check is useful when attacks are new. NHS 111 Wales says that although panic attacks are frightening, they are not dangerous.

body.heading: What can help during an attack?
body.body: The NHS advice is to stay where you are if you can, breathe slowly and deeply, and remind yourself that the attack will pass and is not life threatening. NHS Scotland notes that fighting a panic attack can often make it worse, so accepting the feeling tends to work better than resisting it. Grounding techniques, such as focusing on the senses, can also help.

body.heading: How are repeated attacks treated?
body.body: Cognitive behavioural therapy is the main psychological treatment, and people in England can refer themselves to a talking therapies service or ask a GP to refer them. The NHS lists an SSRI antidepressant as the first medicine, with a tricyclic antidepressant if SSRIs are not suitable. These medicines can take a few weeks to start working, and the NHS advises talking to the GP rather than stopping them without advice. NICE says psychological therapy, medicine and self-help have all been shown to work, and that the benefits of psychological treatment lasted longest.

body.heading: What causes panic disorder, and how is it diagnosed?
body.body: The exact cause of panic disorder is not fully understood, and NHS Scotland says it is probably a combination of physical and psychological factors. A GP asks the person to describe the symptoms, how often they happen and how long they have lasted, and may carry out a physical examination to rule out other conditions.

body.heading: What can people do day to day?
body.body: The NHS suggests regular exercise, calming breathing practice, and cutting down on caffeine, sugary drinks, alcohol and smoking, which can make attacks worse. It also advises against avoiding feared situations altogether, and recommends building up to them gradually.

body.heading: When should someone see a GP?
body.body: The NHS says to speak to a GP if attacks keep happening or affect daily life. If symptoms do not improve, a GP may refer someone to a mental health specialist.

body.heading: Where can someone get urgent help?
body.body: Panic attacks are frightening but pass. If a person feels unable to stay safe, urgent help is open at any time. If you or someone else is in immediate danger, or has been physically harmed, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), which trusts describe as available at any time, for yourself or on someone else's behalf. Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.

nhs-talking-therapies-how-they-work.name: NHS talking therapies and how to self-refer
nhs-talking-therapies-how-they-work.summary: NHS talking therapies offer CBT and counselling for anxiety and depression. In England you can refer yourself, without a GP referral and without a diagnosis.
keyPoints: NHS talking therapies are free psychological treatments for anxiety and depression, such as CBT and counselling.
In England people aged 18 or over can usually refer themselves, without a GP referral and without a diagnosis.
Services are also called IAPT, short for Improving Access to Psychological Therapies.
If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 offer urgent support.

body.heading: What are NHS talking therapies?
body.body: NHS talking therapies services treat common problems such as anxiety and depression with evidence-based psychological treatments. They were previously known as Improving Access to Psychological Therapies, or IAPT, services.

body.heading: What types of help are offered?
body.body: Treatments include cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) and counselling for depression. Formats include a self-help workbook with a therapist's support, an online course, one-to-one sessions in person, by phone or by video, and group sessions. CBT is based on the idea that thoughts, feelings, behaviour and physical sensations are connected, and it helps people notice and challenge unhelpful patterns. It is an active, practical therapy that includes exercises and homework. Counselling for depression is a type of counselling developed for people with depression. Services should offer a choice of in-person or remotely delivered therapy. Talking therapies can also help with mental health problems that come with long-term physical conditions, such as diabetes, cancer or long-term pain.

body.heading: Who can refer themselves?
body.body: The NHS says people can refer themselves directly, without a referral from a GP, or a GP can refer them. Eligibility is mainly about age and location: people aged 18 or over who live in England can self-refer, and some areas also accept 16 and 17 year olds. A diagnosed mental health condition is not needed. Some local services ask people to be registered with a GP in their area, so the local service's own page has the details.

body.heading: What happens after referral?
body.body: People are usually contacted for an initial assessment, often by phone or video. The therapist then recommends a treatment based on the symptoms and how severe they are. Most services begin with a referral check and then a phone assessment, and some arrange a follow-up appointment to complete it. Waiting times vary by area, so the local service can say how long the wait is.

body.heading: What are the limits?
body.body: The self-referral route covers talking therapies rather than medicine, so a GP is still the route for a medicine review or a referral to a psychiatrist. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland run separate systems, so this route describes England.

body.heading: Where can someone get urgent help?
body.body: Talking therapies are not an emergency service. For urgent help, the routes below are open at any time. If you or someone else is in immediate danger, or has been physically harmed, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), which trusts describe as available at any time, for yourself or on someone else's behalf. Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.

supporting-someone-with-a-mental-health-.name: Supporting someone with a mental health problem
supporting-someone-with-a-mental-health-.summary: Listening, asking open questions and offering practical help are the NHS's main suggestions for supporting someone with a mental health problem, without forcing them to talk.
keyPoints: The NHS suggests telling the person you are worried, carrying on as usual, and offering to listen.
Open questions that start with how, what, where or when give the person room to answer in their own words.
The NHS advises against forcing someone to talk or to get help, or going to a GP on their behalf.
If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 offer urgent support.

body.heading: How can you start the conversation?
body.body: The NHS suggests telling the person that you are worried about them. It also suggests carrying on as usual, so the person is not treated differently because of what they are going through. Open questions that start with how, what, where or when are recommended. The NHS says not to force someone to talk to you.

body.heading: What practical help is useful?
body.body: The NHS gives examples of practical help, such as offering to do the shopping or to go with the person to professional appointments. It says not to go to a GP on someone's behalf or to force them to get help. The NHS also says it can be upsetting to hear that someone you care about is in distress, and suggests making time to relax or do something you enjoy. It adds that looking after your own mental wellbeing helps you support others, and that nobody should feel they must cope alone.

body.heading: How can you point someone towards professional help?
body.body: If the difficulties are affecting daily life, the NHS suggests encouraging the person to contact a GP, to get help from NHS 111, or to refer themselves to NHS talking therapies, which is free and does not need an urgent route. Samaritans and Mind are named as sources of guidance for people who are helping. The NHS says someone who cannot wait for a doctor, and cannot cope or keep themselves safe, needs urgent support now.

body.heading: What if the person wants to start talking?
body.body: The NHS guidance for people talking about their own mental health suggests choosing someone they trust who can offer the kind of support they need, and planning what to say. It notes that some people find it easier to talk while walking, travelling in a car or cooking, and that a person does not have to say everything at once. If the person chosen does not feel able to help, the NHS says not to take it personally.

body.heading: Where can someone get urgent help?
body.body: Looking after someone can be hard, and urgent help is open to carers and friends as well as to the person themselves. If you or someone else is in immediate danger, or has been physically harmed, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), which trusts describe as available at any time, for yourself or on someone else's behalf. Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.

loneliness-and-health.name: Loneliness and health: effects and what helps
loneliness-and-health.summary: Severe or long-lasting loneliness can affect mental and physical health, according to the NHS. Staying in touch, joining groups and asking a GP about social prescribing can help.
keyPoints: The NHS says severe or long-lasting loneliness might increase the risk of some physical conditions, such as dementia, and of mental health conditions such as stress, anxiety, low mood or depression.
Regular contact with friends and family, joining a group or club, and volunteering are NHS suggestions for easing loneliness.
A GP can talk about social prescribing, which links people with a link worker for local support.
If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 offer urgent support.

body.heading: What is loneliness, and is it a health issue?
body.body: Loneliness is the distress of feeling alone or disconnected, and it is not the same as spending time by yourself. The NHS says severe or long-lasting loneliness might increase the risk of some physical conditions, such as dementia. It also says it might increase the risk of mental health conditions such as stress, anxiety, low mood or depression. The NHS says loneliness is subjective and can be felt in a busy city or a rural area, online, or while with other people. Significant life events, such as moving home or having a baby, can trigger it.

body.heading: What helps with loneliness?
body.body: NHS suggestions include keeping in touch regularly with friends and family, including through short calls or messages. Joining a group or club is described as a good way to connect and meet people. Volunteering is also described as a good way to meet people. Enjoyable activities such as time outdoors, exercise, reading or podcasts are said to improve wellbeing. The NHS also suggests talking openly about how loneliness feels, and notes that comparing yourself with others, especially on social media, can make you feel lonelier. For older people, the NHS suggests calling or video-chatting with family, joining local groups, starting small conversations when out, and planning things to look forward to.

body.heading: What can a GP or the NHS offer?
body.body: The NHS suggests speaking to a GP about social prescribing, which connects people with a link worker who can point to local support. For stress, anxiety or depression linked to loneliness, NHS talking therapies are available. The NHS advises against using alcohol, cigarettes, gambling or drugs to cope with loneliness, because they can contribute to poor mental health.

body.heading: When should loneliness be taken further?
body.body: If loneliness comes with low mood or anxiety that is lasting or affecting daily life, a GP appointment is the usual route.

body.heading: Where can someone get urgent help?
body.body: Loneliness can make everything feel harder. If it has become overwhelming, people are there to talk at any hour. If you or someone else is in immediate danger, or has been physically harmed, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), which trusts describe as available at any time, for yourself or on someone else's behalf. Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.

grief-and-bereavement-what-to-expect.name: Grief and bereavement: what to expect
grief-and-bereavement-what-to-expect.summary: Grief is a natural response to loss, and the NHS says feelings usually ease gradually. A GP or bereavement service can help when grief is very strong or does not ease.
keyPoints: Grief is a normal response to loss, and the NHS says feelings of sadness should ease gradually over time.
NHS Inform says there is no time limit on grief.
The NHS says to see a GP if someone is struggling to cope, or their own efforts are not helping.
If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 offer urgent support.

body.heading: What does grief feel like?
body.body: Grief can bring shock, numbness, sadness, exhaustion and anger. NHS Inform says there is no time limit on grief and advises against rushing back to usual responsibilities. Delayed grief can be triggered by a later loss, and it is never too late to grieve. An NHS trust lists shock and numbness, overwhelming sadness, tiredness or exhaustion, anger and guilt among common reactions.

body.heading: What can help?
body.body: The NHS suggests talking to a friend, family member or counsellor, regular exercise and regular meals. It advises against using alcohol, cigarettes, gambling or drugs to ease grief, because these can worsen mental health. Bereavement support organisations such as Cruse can help, and talking to others can bring comfort.

body.heading: When is it worth getting help?
body.body: The NHS says sadness should ease gradually with time, but medical help may be needed if someone feels increasingly depressed or anxious. It advises seeing a GP when someone is struggling to cope, has had low mood for more than two weeks, or finds their own efforts are not helping. A GP surgery can refer someone to a therapist or counsellor.

body.heading: Where can bereaved people and children find support?
body.body: The NHS has a bereavement hub, with a section on children and bereavement as well as grief after a bereavement or loss. Cruse Bereavement Support offers a helpline and information on dealing with grief, and Child Bereavement UK and Winston's Wish support bereaved children and families.

body.heading: What is prolonged grief?
body.body: For some people grief does not lessen even after a long time, and the NHS notes this may be a mental health condition called prolonged grief disorder. Signs the NHS lists include difficulty accepting the death and suicidal thoughts, and it advises seeing a GP with these.

body.heading: Where can someone get urgent help?
body.body: If grief brings thoughts of not wanting to go on, urgent help is available. NHS inform in Scotland points to NHS 24 on 111. If you or someone else is in immediate danger, or has been physically harmed, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), which trusts describe as available at any time, for yourself or on someone else's behalf. Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.

menopause-symptoms-and-help-available.name: Menopause: symptoms and the help available
menopause-symptoms-and-help-available.summary: HRT is the main medicine for menopause symptoms, and non-hormone options exist. The NHS says a GP can talk through benefits and risks, and NICE advises offering HRT first for hot flushes.
keyPoints: The NHS calls hormone replacement therapy (HRT) the main medicine for menopause and perimenopause symptoms.
NICE advises offering HRT first for hot flushes and night sweats, after discussing short- and long-term benefits and risks.
Options that do not use hormones include cognitive behavioural therapy, certain medicines for hot flushes, and lubricants for vaginal dryness.
Unscheduled vaginal bleeding should be reported to a GP.

body.heading: What are the symptoms of menopause?
body.body: NICE guidance covers hot flushes and night sweats, vaginal and urinary symptoms, and effects on mood. The perimenopause is the time of change before periods stop, and symptoms can begin then. The NHS lists hot flushes, night sweats, low mood or anxiety, mood swings, brain fog, difficulty sleeping and changes to periods. Others include palpitations, weakening bones, urinary incontinence, headaches and migraines, joint pains, hair thinning, dry skin and reduced sex drive. The NHS says a person may have a number of symptoms, or none. Menopause is confirmed once a person has had no period for 12 months. The NHS says menopause usually affects people between the ages of 45 and 55, though it can happen earlier, and that the perimenopause can last for a few months or several years.

body.heading: What is HRT?
body.body: The NHS says the main medicine for menopause and perimenopause symptoms is hormone replacement therapy, or HRT. Oestrogen comes as skin patches, a gel or spray, implants or tablets. Anyone who still has a womb also needs a progestogen to protect the womb lining. The NHS says a GP will discuss any risks.

body.heading: How soon does treatment work?
body.body: According to the NHS, hot flushes or night sweats often improve within a few weeks. Other symptoms, such as mood changes and vaginal dryness, can take a few months to improve.

body.heading: What are the benefits and risks?
body.body: The NHS says HRT can lower the risk of osteoporosis, the thinning of the bones. Some types of HRT can raise the risk of breast cancer, and blood clots are also a recognised risk. Because benefits and risks differ from person to person, the NHS and NICE both describe a discussion with a clinician.

body.heading: What else is available?
body.body: Low-dose vaginal oestrogen in tablet, cream or ring form can treat vaginal dryness and urinary symptoms. For people who cannot or choose not to take HRT, the NHS lists CBT for mood, sleep and some physical symptoms, and certain medicines for hot flushes. Vaginal lubricants and moisturisers are also used. Regular weight-bearing exercise, cutting down on caffeine, alcohol and spicy food, and stopping smoking can help with hot flushes.

body.heading: When should someone see a GP?
body.body: The NHS says to speak to a GP if symptoms are frequent or severe, or if considering HRT. NICE advises referral to a menopause specialist if treatment does not improve symptoms or causes ongoing side effects. NICE says unscheduled vaginal bleeding should be reported to a GP. The NHS also advises a GP appointment for palpitations, for bleeding that is heavier than before while periods continue, and for any vaginal bleeding after periods have stopped for 12 months or more. Menopause before the age of 40 is called premature menopause or premature ovarian insufficiency, and causes include surgery to remove the ovaries, though sometimes the reason is unknown.

body.heading: Can menopause affect mood?
body.body: NICE suggests considering HRT for low mood that begins around the same time as other menopause symptoms, when the person does not meet the criteria for depression.

body.heading: Where can someone get urgent help?
body.body: Menopause can affect mood and sleep. If low mood becomes severe or there are thoughts of self-harm, help is open at any time. If you or someone else is in immediate danger, or has been physically harmed, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), which trusts describe as available at any time, for yourself or on someone else's behalf. Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.

antenatal-care-on-the-nhs.name: NHS antenatal care: appointments and scans
antenatal-care-on-the-nhs.summary: The NHS offers antenatal appointments with a midwife, two ultrasound scans and optional screening tests. First pregnancies get at least 10 appointments, later ones at least 7.
keyPoints: First-time mothers are offered at least 10 antenatal appointments and 2 ultrasound scans; those who have given birth before are offered at least 7 appointments.
The booking appointment with a midwife is usually the first, and NICE recommends offering it by about 10 weeks of pregnancy.
Screening tests are optional, and NICE says a woman can accept or decline any part of any screening programme.
Exact schedules vary between local maternity services.

body.heading: What antenatal care does the NHS offer?
body.body: The NHS says first-time mothers are offered at least 10 appointments and 2 ultrasound scans. Those who have given birth before are offered at least 7 appointments. The exact schedule varies between local maternity services.

body.heading: What happens at the booking appointment?
body.body: The booking appointment is usually the first appointment with a midwife and can take around an hour. NHS guidance says it is best to attend as early as possible, and NICE recommends offering it by about 10 weeks of pregnancy. At this appointment, NICE recommends that staff discuss and offer screening for infectious diseases (HIV, syphilis and hepatitis B), sickle cell disease and thalassaemia, and fetal anomalies.

body.heading: What checks happen at later appointments?
body.body: Later appointments happen at intervals through pregnancy, and the midwife checks blood pressure, urine, bump size and the baby's movements.

body.heading: What scans are offered?
body.body: The 11 to 14 week scan estimates the due date, checks development and shows whether there is more than one baby; it is sometimes called the dating scan. The 18 to 21 week scan, often called the anomaly or 20-week scan, checks development and screens for rare conditions.

body.heading: Are screening tests compulsory?
body.body: Screening for Down's, Edwards' and Patau's syndromes is offered at the dating scan, and it is the woman's choice whether to have it. NICE says the woman can accept or decline any part of any of the screening programmes offered.

body.heading: What else does antenatal care cover?
body.body: The free flu vaccine is offered in every pregnancy, as is the whooping cough vaccine. Maternity services also give advice on supplements such as folic acid and vitamin D, and the NHS page sets out the amounts. Local trusts vary in the exact schedule and in what they include, for example when tests for gestational diabetes are offered, so the local maternity service's own plan is the reference.

fever-in-children-when-to-get-help.name: Fever and rashes in children: when to get help
fever-in-children-when-to-get-help.summary: Most fevers in children can be looked after at home. The NHS says call 999 for signs such as a stiff neck or a rash that does not fade, and NHS 111 for a baby under 3 months.
keyPoints: The NHS says a child with a fever can usually be looked after at home, with plenty of fluids and regular checks, including overnight.
Call 999 for a stiff neck, a rash that does not fade under a glass, blue, grey or pale skin, being hard to wake, or difficulty breathing.
For a baby under 3 months with a high temperature, the NHS says to call NHS 111.
A GP or NHS 111 should be contacted if a fever lasts 5 days or more.

body.heading: Can a fever be looked after at home?
body.body: The NHS says a child with a fever can usually be looked after at home. It recommends giving plenty of fluids and checking on the child regularly, including overnight.

body.heading: When does a fever need 999?
body.body: The NHS says to call 999 for a stiff neck, a rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed on it, or a first seizure caused by fever. The same list includes cold hands and feet, blue, grey or pale skin, lips or tongue, being drowsy and hard to wake, extreme agitation or confusion, and difficulty breathing. To check a rash, press the side of a clear glass firmly against it; if the spots can still be seen through the glass, the rash is described as non-blanching.

body.heading: When should NHS 111 or the GP be contacted?
body.body: For a baby under 3 months with a high temperature, the NHS says to call NHS 111. For babies aged 3 to 6 months, the NHS also advises calling NHS 111 when the temperature is high. For older children, the NHS advises contacting the GP practice when the temperature is very high, and a GP or NHS 111 when a fever has lasted 5 days or more. Signs of dehydration, such as fewer wet nappies, sunken eyes and no tears when crying, also call for contact with a GP.

body.heading: What about rashes in babies?
body.body: Healthier Together pages say that most baby rashes are harmless and go away on their own, and that dry or peeling skin in the first week or two is normal. Tiny white or yellow spots on the nose or face (milia) usually clear within a few weeks without treatment. Heat rash is not a serious condition and rarely needs specific treatment. Healthier Together lists signs that need urgent help from a health professional: a rash that does not fade under the glass test, pale, blue, mottled or cold skin, fast or laboured breathing, being very sleepy and hard to wake, a fit, and red, hot or swollen skin or redness around the belly button.

falls-in-older-people-reducing-risk.name: Falls in older people and reducing the risk
falls-in-older-people-reducing-risk.summary: Strength and balance exercises and simple changes at home can lower the risk of falls in older people, according to the NHS. NICE recommends offering falls prevention exercise programmes.
keyPoints: The NHS says the risk of falling can be lowered by exercises for strength and balance and by simple changes at home.
NICE guideline NG249 recommends offering a falls prevention exercise programme.
Keeping walkways clear, using stair handrails and wearing well-fitting, non-slip footwear are among the home-safety suggestions.
Regular eye tests are recommended, and the NHS provides free eye tests for people over 60.

body.heading: Why do falls happen?
body.body: The NHS lists muscle weakness that comes with age, conditions that affect mobility or balance (such as arthritis, stroke or Parkinson's), low blood pressure, side effects of some medicines, eyesight or hearing problems, and dementia among the causes of falls. Anyone can have a fall, but it is more likely in older people or those with mobility problems. Some medicines, especially several taken together, can cause drowsiness, light-headedness, faintness or unsteadiness. The NHS advises speaking to a GP or pharmacist if medicines might be affecting balance. Postural hypotension is a drop in blood pressure that usually happens shortly after standing up from lying or sitting, and NICE includes a lying and standing blood pressure check in its falls assessment.

body.heading: What exercise helps?
body.body: The NHS says regular exercises for strength and balance can improve strength and balance and reduce the risk of falls. It lists walking and dancing, and notes evidence that regular tai chi can reduce the risk of falls. Programmes are described as best when tailored to the individual and overseen by a trained professional.

body.heading: What can be changed at home?
body.body: Suggestions include keeping walkways clear, using handrails on stairs, and wearing non-slip, well-fitting footwear. Regular eye tests are recommended, and free NHS eye tests are available to people over 60.

body.heading: What does NICE recommend?
body.body: NICE guideline NG249 covers falls assessment and prevention in older people and in people aged 50 and over at higher risk, and recommends offering a falls prevention exercise programme.

body.heading: What can a GP or falls team do?
body.body: The NHS lists the GP's role as checking for problems such as muscle weakness, osteoporosis and eyesight problems, and reviewing medicines. Some areas have a falls team that offers a full assessment to older people who have fallen or are at high risk, and availability varies, so a GP can say what exists locally.

body.heading: What does the NHS advise after a fall?
body.body: Advice after a fall includes calling for help, using a lifeline alarm if there is one, and keeping warm by covering up with a rug, blanket or towel. It also includes moving the parts of the body that do not hurt, and getting up gradually if able. Someone who is hurt or cannot get up should seek medical help.

hearing-loss-causes-tests-and-help.name: Hearing loss: causes, tests and what helps
hearing-loss-causes-tests-and-help.summary: Gradual hearing loss is common and a GP can arrange hearing tests. Sudden hearing loss in one or both ears needs an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111, according to the NHS.
keyPoints: Gradual hearing loss in both ears is usually linked to ageing or long-term exposure to loud noise.
A GP can examine the ears and refer to an audiologist or an ENT specialist for tests.
Sudden hearing loss in one or both ears needs an urgent GP appointment or help from NHS 111, and should not be left to see if it improves.
NHS hearing aids are free.

body.heading: What causes hearing loss?
body.body: Gradual hearing loss in both ears is usually linked to ageing or to damage from loud noise over many years. Earwax, ear infections and a perforated eardrum are other common causes. NHS inform describes two types: sensorineural, from damage to the inner ear's hair cells or the hearing nerve, and conductive, where sound cannot pass to the inner ear, often because of earwax, glue ear or fluid from an infection.

body.heading: What are the signs of hearing loss?
body.body: One hospital audiology service lists difficulty hearing the television at a level that suits others, struggling to understand speech, and difficulty following speech in noise as reasons to ask for a test.

body.heading: When should someone see a GP?
body.body: The NHS advises seeing a GP for hearing that seems to be getting worse, or that has not returned after treatment for an ear infection or earwax. Some pharmacies and opticians also offer a free hearing test.

body.heading: What happens at the GP?
body.body: A GP can check for problems such as earwax or infection and may refer to an audiologist or an ENT specialist for further tests. If the GP finds no obvious cause, the person should be referred for a full assessment, and some large pharmacies and opticians have audiologists who test adults. At the audiology appointment, the audiologist typically asks about hearing history and health, looks in the ears with an otoscope, and runs a test in which the person wears headphones and presses a button when a sound is heard. The test shows which pitches are affected and by how much.

body.heading: What if hearing is lost suddenly?
body.body: The NHS says to ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 for sudden hearing loss in one or both ears. If neither is reachable, the nearest accident and emergency department is the route. Waiting to see whether it recovers on its own is not advised, because the loss can be permanent. For sudden sensorineural loss the cause is often never found, and the usual treatment is steroids, which are most likely to help when given soon after the loss starts.

body.heading: What helps with permanent hearing loss and tinnitus?
body.body: For tinnitus, the first person to speak to is the GP, who may refer to an ENT surgeon or an audiovestibular physician. Treatable causes such as earwax or infection can often be dealt with by a GP, while permanent loss is usually managed with hearing aids. Hearing aids do not make hearing perfect, but they make sounds louder and clearer, and NHS hearing aids are free.

dementia-early-signs-and-assessment.name: Dementia: early signs and how it is assessed
dementia-early-signs-and-assessment.summary: Early signs of dementia include memory loss, trouble with familiar tasks and confusion about time or place. A GP starts the assessment, and a memory clinic may confirm the diagnosis.
keyPoints: The NHS lists memory loss, difficulty concentrating, trouble with familiar daily tasks, struggling to follow conversations, confusion about time and place, and mood changes as common early symptoms.
Memory can be affected by stress, tiredness, certain illnesses and medicines, so the NHS suggests a GP visit for someone who is becoming increasingly forgetful, particularly over 65.
NICE recommends a history from the person and someone who knows them, a physical examination, and blood and urine tests to look for reversible causes.
A person may be referred to a memory clinic once reversible causes have been looked into and dementia is still suspected.

body.heading: What are the early signs?
body.body: The NHS says some common early symptoms may appear some time before a diagnosis. They include memory loss, difficulty concentrating, trouble with familiar daily tasks, struggling to follow conversations, confusion about time and place, and mood changes. Early symptoms are often mild and gradual, and family and friends may not notice them or take them seriously for some time. Alzheimer's disease is the most common form of dementia, and vascular dementia is usually the second most common.

body.heading: Is forgetfulness always dementia?
body.body: The NHS says it is normal for memory to be affected by stress, tiredness, certain illnesses and medicines. It suggests talking to a GP if someone is becoming increasingly forgetful, particularly if they are over 65.

body.heading: What happens at the GP?
body.body: NICE says a GP or other non-specialist should take a history of cognitive, behavioural and psychological symptoms and their effect on daily life, from the person and, if possible, from someone who knows them well. If dementia is still suspected, NICE recommends a physical examination and blood and urine tests to rule out reversible causes. It also recommends cognitive testing with a validated brief tool, and says a normal screening result alone should not rule dementia out. The NHS says there is no single test for dementia, and that diagnosis rests on a combination of assessments and tests. Cognitive tests usually come first, and brain scans are often used once simpler tests have ruled out other problems.

body.heading: When is a memory clinic involved?
body.body: The person should be referred to a memory clinic or community old age psychiatry service once reversible causes, such as delirium, depression, sensory impairment or the effects of medicines, have been looked into and dementia is still suspected. The specialist assessment includes a neurological examination and cognitive testing, and a dementia subtype is diagnosed where possible. The first memory clinic appointment is usually long, and people are asked to bring someone who knows them well. After a diagnosis, some clinics arrange a follow-up with a specialist nurse to answer questions and discuss support, and the NHS says to give yourself time to adjust.

body.heading: What if it is unclear whether it is delirium or dementia?
body.body: NICE says that when it is unclear whether someone has delirium, dementia or both, the delirium is treated first. Delirium is a sudden state of confusion, often linked to illness, and needs prompt medical attention; NHS 111 or a GP is the usual route, or 999 in an emergency.
